title: Are all GPA functions the same?
text:
A look at the results and the speed to obtain them from several Generalized Procrustes Analysis functions in R.





library(geomorph)

# make a latticed cube
vert <- 5
template <- expand.grid(1:vert, 1:vert, 1:vert)
colnames(template) <- c("x", "y", "z")

# add points for n specimens
n <- 50
LM <- LMlist <- lapply(seq_len(n), function(.){
  as.matrix(template + rnorm(length(template),
                   mean = 0, sd = 0.3))
})

LM <- simplify2array(LM)
plotAllSpecimens(LM)




system.time(GPA1 <- gpagen(LM, print.progress = FALSE))

   user  system elapsed 
  0.009   0.002   0.013 

plot(GPA1)




library(Morpho)
system.time(GPA2 <- ProcGPA(LM))

   user  system elapsed 
  0.037   0.001   0.040 

plotAllSpecimens(GPA2$rotated)




two.b.pls(GPA1$coords, GPA2$rotated, print.progress = FALSE)

Data in either A1 or A2 do not have names.  It is assumed data in both A1 and A2 are ordered the same.



Call:
two.b.pls(A1 = GPA1$coords, A2 = GPA2$rotated, print.progress = FALSE) 



r-PLS: 1

Effect Size (Z): 4.3652

P-value: 0.001

Based on 1000 random permutations


Although they seem perfectly correlated, you might notice by spinning the plots a slight difference in the scatter. With gpagen, the default is to project configurations into a space tanget to shape space. The procGPA function does not do this. So, gpagen scatter looks more planar and procGPA more hemispherical at each point. We can update this so they are the same.

system.time(GPA1 <- gpagen(LM, print.progress = FALSE, Proj = FALSE))

   user  system elapsed 
  0.004   0.000   0.004 

plot(GPA1)




two.b.pls(GPA1$coords, GPA2$rotated, print.progress = FALSE)

Data in either A1 or A2 do not have names.  It is assumed data in both A1 and A2 are ordered the same.



Call:
two.b.pls(A1 = GPA1$coords, A2 = GPA2$rotated, print.progress = FALSE) 



r-PLS: 1

Effect Size (Z): 4.3551

P-value: 0.001

Based on 1000 random permutations






Similar results
gpagen is faster





library(shapes)
system.time(GPA3 <- procGPA(LM))

   user  system elapsed 
  0.186   0.006   0.194 

plotAllSpecimens(GPA2$rotated)




two.b.pls(GPA1$coords, GPA3$rotated, print.progress = FALSE)

Data in either A1 or A2 do not have names.  It is assumed data in both A1 and A2 are ordered the same.



Call:

r-PLS: 1

Based on 1000 random permutations

title: Are all GPA functions the same?
text:
Simulated Examples for gpagen
Concerning computational efficiency in GPA, there are two “big data” attributes for which to be concerned with geometric morphometric (GM) data: wide data, which is a large number of landmarks (including semilandmarks); and long data, which is a large set of landmark configurations (specimens). These should be studied independently in comparative computational assessments, to determine if attempted optimization of analytical functions is successful only in certain regards. To generate data, we use an automated function, which generates a shape template that is a grid formed along \(x\) and \(y\) axes, with the height of points inversely associated with distance from center, creating a dome-like figure. The fraction of sliding semilandmarks and level of variation for isotropic random points applied to the template can also be varied. 

get.array <- function(grid.n, spec.n, sdev= 0.5, f.surf = 0.5){
  x <- seq(0:grid.n) - mean(seq(0:grid.n))
  coord.t <- as.data.frame(expand.grid(x, x))
  colnames(coord.t) <- c("x", "y")
  coord.t$z <- apply(coord.t, 1, function(y) 0.5*(sqrt(max(x)^2) - sqrt(sum(y^2))))
  surf <- which(coord.t$z > quantile(coord.t$z, 1- f.surf))
  fixed <- (1:nrow(coord.t))[-surf]
  npk <- length(as.matrix(coord.t))
  coords <- lapply(1:spec.n, function(.) coord.t + rnorm(npk, sd = sdev))
  dims <- dim(coords[[1]])
  coords <- array(unlist(coords), c(dims, spec.n))
  list(template = coord.t, 
       coords = coords, 
       surf = surf, fixed = fixed)
}

title: Are all GPA functions the same?
text:
Wide data example
Below is an example template of a dome from a \(32 \times 32\) grid, with 50% of the landmarks as sliders (shown in red), with 20 specimens, created with this function. 

ex1 <- get.array(32, 20, 0.3, 0.5)


Before GPA

colors <- rep(1, nrow(ex1$template))
colors[ex1$surf] <- 2
plotAllSpecimens(ex1$coords,
                 plot_param = list(mean.bg = colors))







After GPA

GPA1 <- gpagen(ex1$coords, surf = ex1$surf, max.iter = 2, print.progress = FALSE)

plot(GPA1, plot_param = list(mean.bg = colors))

title: How fast is your Procrustes ANOVA?
text:
If you have high-dimensional shape data, Procrustes ANOVA to compare group means is probably pretty common. Becuase a Procrustes ANOVA requires a permutation procedure, with thousands of permutations, it can take a long time.
But not all functions are the same! Here we compare several that might be used by researchers who have high-dimensional (HD) shape data: RRPP::lm.rrpp & RRPP::anova.lm.rrpp, vegan::adonis2, and PERMANOVA::PERMANOVA.



Single core analysis. Not every function has parallel options, so for functions where it is an option, they will be constrained to use 1 core.
1,000 random permutations. Except in one case we only use 10, and it will be obvious why.
ANOVA must be performed. This means for some functions first fitting many linear models then using anova(). Others perform ANOVA inherently.
Data formatting. Any formatting is done prior to analysis but not counted as part of the analysis for measuring computation time.





library(geomorph)

# make a latticed cube
vert <- 8
template <- expand.grid(1:vert, 1:vert, 1:vert)
colnames(template) <- c("x", "y", "z")

# Groups
ng <- 10
nw <- 10
group <- factor(rep(1:ng, each = nw))
n <- length(group)

# add points for n specimens

LMlist <- lapply(seq_len(n), function(.){
  as.matrix(template + rnorm(length(template),
                   mean = 0, sd = 0.3))
})




LMa <- simplify2array(LMlist)
GPA <- gpagen(LMa, print.progress = FALSE)
plot(GPA)










Y <- two.d.array(GPA$coords)
dim(Y)

[1]  100 1536

system.time(
  {fit1 <- lm.rrpp(Y ~ group, 
                 iter = 999,
                 Parallel = 1,
                 turbo = TRUE);
  AOV1 <- anova(fit1)}
)

   user  system elapsed 
  0.164   0.014   0.185 

AOV1

All results are similar. The mvabund \(F\)-statistics are different because they are like the sum of \(p\) \(F\)-statistics rather than a single \(F\)-statistic calculated from the sum of \(p\) \(SS\) values.
RRPP and vegan are faster than the others.
It probably is not fair to include mvabund::anova.manylm because it perfoms more of a MANOVA analysis, which requires inverting residual covariance matrices.
Regardless, PERMANOVA::PERMANOVA is comparatively much slower.




Let’s see how the top two functions (in terms of computational efficiency) perform as we increase the amount of data.

nscape <- seq(10, 50, 10)

Result <- sapply(nscape, function(ng){
  group <- factor(rep(1:ng, each = nw))
  n <- length(group)
  LMlist <- lapply(seq_len(n), function(.){
    as.matrix(template + 
                rnorm(length(template),
                mean = 0, sd = 0.3))
  })
  LMa <- simplify2array(LMlist)
  GPA <- gpagen(LMa, 
                print.progress = FALSE)
  Y <- two.d.array(GPA$coords)
  D <- dist(Y)
  df <- rrpp.data.frame(group = group,
                        Y = Y)
  
  t_RRPP <- system.time(
    {fit1 <- lm.rrpp(Y ~ group, 
                     iter = 999,
                     Parallel = 1,
                     turbo = TRUE,
                     data = df);
    AOV1 <- anova(fit1)}
  )[[3]]
  
  t_adonis <- system.time(
    AOV2 <- adonis2(D ~ group,
                    permutations = 999,
                    parallel = 1))[[3]]
  
  c(n = n, t_RRPP = t_RRPP, 
    t_adonis = t_adonis)
  
})

plot(Result[1, ], Result[3,],
     type = "o", pch = 16, col = 2,
     lwd = 2, 
     xlab = "n", ylab = "Time, s")
points(Result[1, ], Result[2,], lwd = 2,
       type = "o", pch = 16, col = 4)
legend("topleft", c("vegan", "RRPP"),
       lty = 1, lwd = 2, 
       pch = 16, col = c(2, 4))








This is not surprising because vegan::adonis2 uses \(n \times n\) distance matrices as data and \(n \times n\) hat matrices for estimates. Even though it also uses Hadamard products (element-wise products between squared, centered distance and hat matrices), which are computationally quicker than matrix products, the matrices grow exponentially with a linear increase in \(n\). By contrast, RRPP::lm.rrpp uses sparse-matrix forms of \(\mathbf{Q}\) matrices from \(\mathbf{QR}\) decomposition of a linear model design matrix, \(\mathbf{X}\) and obtains the matrix product, \(\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Y}\). The sum of squared values from this product is the same as the summed squared values from the Hadamard products, but fewer calculations are needed, especially, comparatively, as \(n\) increases.

How fast is your Procrustes ANOVA?
text:
All results are similar. The mvabund \(F\)-statistics are different because they are like the sum of \(p\) \(F\)-statistics rather than a single \(F\)-statistic calculated from the sum of \(p\) \(SS\) values.
RRPP and vegan are faster than the others.
It probably is not fair to include mvabund::anova.manylm because it perfoms more of a MANOVA analysis, which requires inverting residual covariance matrices.
Regardless, PERMANOVA::PERMANOVA is comparatively much slower.

title: How fast is your Procrustes ANOVA?
text:
Let’s see how the top two functions (in terms of computational efficiency) perform as we increase the amount of data.

nscape <- seq(10, 50, 10)

Result <- sapply(nscape, function(ng){
  group <- factor(rep(1:ng, each = nw))
  n <- length(group)
  LMlist <- lapply(seq_len(n), function(.){
    as.matrix(template + 
                rnorm(length(template),
                mean = 0, sd = 0.3))
  })
  LMa <- simplify2array(LMlist)
  GPA <- gpagen(LMa, 
                print.progress = FALSE)
  Y <- two.d.array(GPA$coords)
  D <- dist(Y)
  df <- rrpp.data.frame(group = group,
                        Y = Y)
  
  t_RRPP <- system.time(
    {fit1 <- lm.rrpp(Y ~ group, 
                     iter = 999,
                     Parallel = 1,
                     turbo = TRUE,
                     data = df);
    AOV1 <- anova(fit1)}
  )[[3]]
  
  t_adonis <- system.time(
    AOV2 <- adonis2(D ~ group,
                    permutations = 999,
                    parallel = 1))[[3]]
  
  c(n = n, t_RRPP = t_RRPP, 
    t_adonis = t_adonis)
  
})

plot(Result[1, ], Result[3,],
     type = "o", pch = 16, col = 2,
     lwd = 2, 
     xlab = "n", ylab = "Time, s")
points(Result[1, ], Result[2,], lwd = 2,
       type = "o", pch = 16, col = 4)
legend("topleft", c("vegan", "RRPP"),
       lty = 1, lwd = 2, 
       pch = 16, col = c(2, 4))








This is not surprising because vegan::adonis2 uses \(n \times n\) distance matrices as data and \(n \times n\) hat matrices for estimates. Even though it also uses Hadamard products (element-wise products between squared, centered distance and hat matrices), which are computationally quicker than matrix products, the matrices grow exponentially with a linear increase in \(n\). By contrast, RRPP::lm.rrpp uses sparse-matrix forms of \(\mathbf{Q}\) matrices from \(\mathbf{QR}\) decomposition of a linear model design matrix, \(\mathbf{X}\) and obtains the matrix product, \(\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Y}\). The sum of squared values from this product is the same as the summed squared values from the Hadamard products, but fewer calculations are needed, especially, comparatively, as \(n\) increases.
